item.text:
Short answer: **vegetation is probably getting better, but the public evidence is still weak; fire does not clearly look lower in the same period.**

What I found:
EBTL says it had started restoration **by October 1, 2022** and that its first three years focused on a native nursery, water-flow learning, planting, invasive removal, and natural regeneration. It also says it has raised **130+ native plant species** and about **15,000 saplings**. That is a good sign that vegetation work is progressing. But I did **not** find a public before/after dataset for EBTL itself, such as yearly canopy cover, NDVI, plant survival, or species richness, so I cannot prove how much the vegetation has improved. Sources: [Nithin Kamath post](https://nithinkamath.me/blog/elephants-by-the-lake.md/), [EBTL About](https://ebtl.earth/about/), [EBTL Restoration Project](https://ebtl.earth/restoration-project/).

For fire, I did **not** find public fire records just for EBTL. The best public proxy I found is **Krishnagiri district** data from Global Forest Watch. That shows **346 VIIRS fire alerts between July 4, 2022 and June 29, 2026**, and says **2023** had the highest tree-cover loss from fire in the district during 2001-2025, with **64 ha** lost that year. So, at least at district scale, fire has **not clearly gone down** during the EBTL restoration years; it was still active and seems to have spiked in 2023. Source: [Global Forest Watch, Krishnagiri dashboard](https://www.globalforestwatch.org/dashboards/country/IND/31/11/?location=WyJjb3VudHJ5IiwiSU5EIiwiMzEiLCIxMSJd&).

What is missing:
EBTL’s exact mapped boundary, yearly vegetation indicators, and an on-site fire log or burned-area record. Without those, the vegetation answer is partly an **estimate**, and the fire answer is only a **regional proxy**, not proof for the EBTL property itself.
